meta.title: C172 JT-A Trainer
meta.subtitle: OSM Cessna 172R/S diesel technical study addon
meta.notice: Study aid only. Use current POH/AFM, OSM procedures, instructor guidance, and approved checklists for operation.

quickFacts.label: Fuel
quickFacts.value: 47.6 US gal total, 44.6 US gal usable

quickFacts.label: Electrical
quickFacts.value: 28 V / 60 A alternator, 24 V main battery, 24 V standby battery

hotspots.label: Master / Avionics
hotspots.summary: Main electrical control area for battery, alternator, and avionics buses.
details: BAT supplies the main bus from the aircraft battery.
ALT brings the alternator online when the engine is running.
Avionics Bus 1 and Bus 2 power the installed avionics equipment.
hotspots.check: Know which items remain available on essential/standby power after failures.

hotspots.label: Standby Battery
hotspots.summary: Independent 24 V standby source connected to the essential bus.
details: Used to support essential equipment during selected electrical failures.
The diesel installation also uses backup power logic for FADEC A.
hotspots.check: Treat endurance values as POH/AFM-specific. The trainer marks this as a study reminder, not a checklist.

hotspots.label: PFD
hotspots.summary: Primary flight display for attitude, air data, navigation, and engine strip awareness.
details: Failure modes include display failure, ADC/AHRS loss, magnetometer loss, or engine data loss.
Reversionary mode can present essential information on the remaining display.
hotspots.check: Be able to explain what changes when AHRS, ADC, or display information is lost.

hotspots.label: MFD / Engine
hotspots.summary: Multi-function display with map, engine indications, systems information, and G1000 pages.
details: Engine strip indications are central for diesel system monitoring.
Electrical voltage, current, fuel quantity, and engine parameters are part of the technical scan.
hotspots.check: Use this area for future clickable G1000 failure and indication training.

hotspots.label: Engine Master
hotspots.summary: Engine master switch controls engine/FADEC operating state.
details: The JT-A uses FADEC and single-lever style engine management.
Engine operation depends on correct FADEC power, fuel, and sensor logic.
hotspots.check: Good oral topic: explain why diesel/FADEC operation differs from a conventional avgas C172.

hotspots.label: FADEC Test / Force B
hotspots.summary: FADEC test and backup channel controls.
details: FADEC A and B provide engine control channels.
The pre-takeoff FADEC test verifies automatic control logic before flight.
hotspots.check: Later we can model the exact test sequence using approved procedures.

hotspots.label: Circuit Breaker Panel
hotspots.summary: Cockpit circuit breaker panel for protected electrical loads.
details: Groups include electrical buses, avionics, FADEC, lights, flaps, and instruments.
Breaker logic is a future high-value simulator layer.
hotspots.check: Use the cockpit card as the visual source for exact breaker names and positions.

hotspots.label: Wing Flaps
hotspots.summary: Electric flap selector with 10, 20, and 30 degree positions.
details: Single slotted Fowler flaps are driven by one electric motor in the right wing.
Published flap speed limits and landing configurations are core technical test items.
hotspots.check: Know the max speeds for flap 10 and flap 20/30.

hotspots.label: Cabin Heat / Air
details: Ram air enters through wing openings and can be directed through cabin nozzles.
Heated air is associated with engine cooling air and must be treated carefully in smoke, fire, or CO scenarios.
hotspots.check: Oral prompt: when should cabin heat/air not be used?

hotspots.label: Fuel Shutoff
hotspots.summary: Fuel shutoff control on the center pedestal.
details: This is part of engine securing logic in abnormal procedures.
The trainer keeps responses high-level and avoids checklist replacement.
hotspots.check: Study link: engine fire, engine failure, and securing engine memory items.

hotspots.label: Fuel Selector
hotspots.summary: Fuel selector with BOTH, LEFT, and RIGHT positions.
details: Normal fuel management and imbalance awareness are part of system knowledge.
Fuel quantity and LOW FUEL logic should be cross-checked with the G1000 indications.
hotspots.check: Be able to explain what changes when LEFT or RIGHT is selected.

systems.name: Fuel
systems.headline: Two wing tanks feed the diesel engine through selector, pumps, filtration, high-pressure delivery, and return logic.
learn: Two tanks: 23.8 US gal each, 47.6 US gal total.
Usable fuel: 22.3 US gal each, 44.6 US gal total.
Fuel reaches the engine through gravity/feed path support plus electric and engine-driven pumping.
Approved fuel notes in the course: Jet A-1 and Jet A; do not fuel with AVGAS.
oral: Explain the fuel path from tank to injector.
What happens to system risk if the fuel filter becomes restricted?
What changes when only LEFT or only RIGHT is selected?

systems.name: Engine / FADEC
systems.headline: A liquid-cooled turbocharged diesel engine is controlled by FADEC with A/B channel logic.
learn: TAE 125-02-114, four-cylinder, liquid-cooled, turbocharged engine.
155 BHP at 2300 RPM through a reduction gearbox.
Compression ignition: no conventional spark ignition system.
FADEC power and backup logic are central oral-test topics.
oral: Explain what FADEC does in simple terms.
Why does this engine not use magnetos?
What is the purpose of the FADEC test before takeoff?

systems.name: Electrical
systems.headline: A 28 V alternator, main battery, standby battery, buses, switches, and breakers supply aircraft loads.
learn: Alternator: 28 V, 60 A.
Main battery: 24 V, installed forward of the firewall area.
Standby battery: 24 V, connected to essential bus logic.
Electrical failures are best learned through bus/load relationships.
oral: Explain normal alternator and battery roles.
What is the purpose of the standby battery?
What cockpit indications would you expect during low-voltage operation?

systems.name: Cooling / Oil / Gearbox
systems.headline: Liquid cooling, oil quantity, and gearbox oil checks are key diesel-specific handling items.
learn: Cooling circuit changes with temperature through thermostat logic.
Course note: small circuit below 84 C, transition 84-94 C, large circuit 94-105 C.
Oil quantity range: 4.5-6 L.
Gearbox oil quantity is checked before flight.
oral: Why does coolant temperature matter for diesel engine operation?
What oil quantity range should you know?
What is checked at the gearbox before flight?

systems.name: Airframe / Controls
systems.headline: Flaps, controls, landing gear, brakes, doors, and limitation numbers form the aircraft-handling foundation.
learn: Flaps are electrically operated single slotted Fowler flaps.
Flap positions: 10, 20, and 30 degrees.
Know normal and utility category weight/load-factor differences.
Landing technique varies with flap setting, wind, and surface.
oral: When might flap 20 be preferred over full flap?
What is the difference between normal and utility category?

systems.name: G1000 / Instruments
systems.headline: PFD, MFD, LRUs, ADC/AHRS, magnetometer, engine data, and reversionary mode tie the cockpit together.
learn: PFD and MFD failure modes must be recognized quickly.
AHRS, ADC, magnetometer, GEA, NAV/COM, and audio panel failures have different symptoms.
Engine and electrical indications support technical decision-making.
Traffic, AoA, and map functions are useful but do not replace basic scan.
oral: Explain what happens after a display failure.
What information is lost with ADC failure?
How would you recognize AHRS failure?

failures.title: LOW VOLTS / alternator not carrying load
failures.indication: Low-voltage warning, battery discharge trend, reduced electrical endurance.
failures.risk: Progressive loss of electrical equipment if power source management is not corrected.
failures.studyResponse: Study note: identify source/load problem, preserve essential equipment, and use approved checklist.

failures.title: Restricted fuel filter
failures.indication: Possible power instability, abnormal fuel pressure/flow logic, or engine roughness depending on severity.
failures.risk: Reduced fuel delivery to high-pressure side and engine power reliability concern.
failures.studyResponse: Study note: treat as fuel/engine abnormality and follow approved procedures.

failures.title: FADEC channel problem
failures.indication: FADEC caution/warning logic and possible channel reversion depending on fault.
failures.risk: Reduced redundancy or degraded engine control logic.
failures.studyResponse: Study note: understand A/B channel purpose and use the aircraft checklist, not memory guesses.

failures.title: High coolant temperature
failures.indication: Coolant temperature rising toward or beyond normal range.
failures.risk: Thermal stress, possible engine limitation exceedance, or power management issue.
failures.studyResponse: Study note: reduce thermal load as directed by approved procedures and monitor trend.

oralQuestions.prompt: Explain the complete fuel path from tank to injector.
oralQuestions.model: Fuel is stored in the wing tanks, selected through the fuel selector, then routed through the low-pressure/feed side including pump and filter functions before engine-driven/high-pressure delivery supplies the common rail and injectors. Return logic routes unused fuel back through the system as designed.

oralQuestions.prompt: Why is the JT-A engine different from a normal avgas C172 engine?
oralQuestions.model: It is a diesel/Jet-A installation with compression ignition, FADEC control, liquid cooling, turbocharging, a reduction gearbox, and single-lever style power management instead of mixture/prop/magneto handling.

oralQuestions.prompt: What are the main electrical power sources?
oralQuestions.model: The system uses a 28 V alternator, 24 V main battery, and 24 V standby battery. The alternator normally carries the load in flight, the main battery supports starting and backup supply, and the standby battery supports essential bus logic.

oralQuestions.prompt: Describe the flap system and important speeds.
oralQuestions.model: The aircraft has electrically operated single slotted Fowler flaps with 10, 20, and 30 degree positions. Course limits include 110 KIAS for flap 10 and 85 KIAS for flap 20/30.

oralQuestions.prompt: When should cabin heat or cabin air not be used?
oralQuestions.model: Study note: do not use cabin heat/air in scenarios such as engine fire, electrical fire, suspected carbon monoxide, strange smell, dizziness, or as otherwise directed by approved procedures.

memoryDrill.title: Fuel Path Memory
memoryDrill.prompt: Click the fuel components in the most logical tank-to-engine order.
